systems-center-of-mass-s1.title: A wrench sliding across ice
systems-center-of-mass-s1.html: A wrench is given a spin and a shove across smooth, level ice. A camera above records it every 0.20 s. Most of its mass is in the steel head; the black dot marks the light end of the handle.

systems-center-of-mass-s2.title: Three clamps on a meterstick
systems-center-of-mass-s2.html:
A student clamps three small masses to a meterstick of negligible mass. Each clamp is small enough to treat as a point object at the position shown, measured from the 0 end of the stick.

Masses and positions on the stick
ClampMass (kg)Position (m)
10.200.10
20.300.50
30.700.90

forces-fbd-s1.title: A loaded sled slowing down
forces-fbd-s1.html: A sled loaded with firewood moves to the right across level snow. A person ahead of it pulls a horizontal rope, but the sled is slowing down. The snow rubs on the sled's runners. Air resistance is negligible.

forces-fbd-s2.title: A bucket raised on a rope
forces-fbd-s2.html: A 4.0 kg bucket of sand hangs from a single rope that runs over a pulley on the ceiling to a person's hand. The person pulls the rope, raising the bucket straight up at a constant speed. Air resistance is negligible.

third-law-s1.title: Two blocks pushed together
third-law-s1.html: A student pushes a 6.0 kg block to the right with a 24 N horizontal force. The 6.0 kg block pushes a 2.0 kg block that sits against it. The floor is frictionless, and both blocks speed up together.

third-law-s2.title: A truck towing a car
third-law-s2.html: A truck tows a car along a level road with a light tow rope. The truck and the car speed up together to the right. Treat the rope as an ideal string.

first-law-s1.title: A sign hung from two cords
first-law-s1.html: A 5.0 kg sign hangs at rest from two identical light cords. Each cord makes a 30° angle with the horizontal. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

first-law-s2.title: A crate pushed across a warehouse floor
first-law-s2.html:
A worker pushes a 40 kg crate across a level floor with a horizontal force. A motion detector records the crate's velocity, and a force sensor between the worker's hands and the crate records the push. The friction from the floor is 120 N throughout. At 2.0 s the worker starts pushing harder.

Push and velocity of the crate
Time (s)Push (N)Velocity (m/s)
0.01200.80
1.01200.80
2.01200.80
3.01501.55
4.01502.30

second-law-s1.title: A cart pulled by a hanging block
second-law-s1.html: A 0.80 kg cart on a level track is tied to a light string that runs over a light, frictionless pulley to a hanging 0.20 kg block. Friction on the cart is negligible. The block is released from rest. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

second-law-s2.title: Acceleration against net force
second-law-s2.html:
Students pull a 2.0 kg cart along a level, low-friction track with a force sensor and measure its acceleration with a motion detector. They also repeat one trial with 2.0 kg of bricks loaded onto the cart.

Net force on the cart and its acceleration
TrialMass of cart and load (kg)Net force (N)Acceleration (m/s²)
12.01.00.51
22.02.00.98
32.03.01.52
42.04.02.01

gravitational-force-s1.title: Scale readings during an elevator ride
gravitational-force-s1.html:
A 60 kg student stands on a bathroom scale in an elevator that starts at rest on the ground floor and stops at rest on an upper floor. She records the scale reading at several times. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

Scale reading during the ride
Time (s)Scale reading (N)
0.0588
2.0660
4.0588
8.0588
10.0516

gravitational-force-s2.title: Weighing a lander on Mars
gravitational-force-s2.html:
A robotic lander has a mass of 300 kg. Mars has a mass of 6.42 × 10²³ kg and a radius of 3.39 × 10⁶ m. Earth has a mass of 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and a radius of 6.37 × 10⁶ m. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

The size of the gravitational force between two objects is |Fg| = Gm₁m₂/r², where r is the distance between their centers. The gravitational field at a point is g = Fg/m.

friction-s1.title: Pushing a crate that starts at rest
friction-s1.html:
A 25 kg crate rests on a level warehouse floor. A worker pushes it horizontally, slowly increasing the push, while a force sensor records the push and a motion detector reports whether the crate moves. Once it slides, the worker adjusts the push to keep the crate sliding at a constant speed. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

Push on the crate and its motion
Push (N)Crate
50at rest
75at rest
140at rest
147just starts to slide
98sliding at constant speed

friction-s2.title: A crate resting on a ramp
friction-s2.html: A 20.0 kg wooden crate rests without sliding on a ramp tilted at θ = 25.0° above the horizontal. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

spring-forces-s1.title: Stretching a spring with hanging masses
spring-forces-s1.html:
A student hangs a light spring from a clamp and hangs slotted masses from its lower end. For each mass, once the mass hangs at rest, she measures how far the spring has stretched from its relaxed length with a meterstick. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

Hanging mass and stretch of the spring
Hanging mass (kg)Stretch (m)
0.0500.020
0.1000.040
0.1500.061

spring-forces-s2.title: A cart held against a compressed spring
spring-forces-s2.html: A 0.50 kg cart on a level, frictionless track is attached to an ideal spring of spring constant 80 N/m whose other end is fixed to a wall. A student pushes the cart toward the wall, compressing the spring by 0.15 m, and holds it at rest. Take the direction away from the wall as positive.

circular-motion-s1.title: A puck on a string
circular-motion-s1.html: A 0.40 kg puck slides in a horizontal circle of radius 0.50 m on a frictionless table, held by a light string tied to a peg at the center. It makes 2.0 revolutions each second at a constant speed.

circular-motion-s2.title: A car over a hill
circular-motion-s2.html: A 1200 kg car drives over the crest of a rounded hill at a constant speed of 12 m/s. Near the crest the road follows a vertical circle of radius 45 m. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

items.q: Which statement describes the motion of the wrench's center of mass across the ice?
options: It moves along a straight line, covering equal distances in equal times
It moves along a wavy path that follows the swinging handle
It curves toward the heavy head a little more in each picture
It speeds up each time the wrench completes half a turn

items.q: Between 0.00 s and 0.80 s the wrench's center of mass moves 2.4 m along the dashed line. What is its average speed, in m/s?

mistakes.why: Value: that divides by one 0.20 s interval. The 2.4 m is covered over four intervals, 0.80 s in all.

items.q: A second student tracks the black dot at the end of the handle instead of the center of mass. What will she find?
options: The dot's displacement changes from one 0.20 s interval to the next
The dot moves the same distance as the center of mass in each interval
The dot stays at the same distance ahead of the center of mass
The dot moves in a straight line, parallel to the dashed line

items.q: Why is the wrench's center of mass much closer to the head than to the end of the handle?
options: More of the wrench's mass is in the head
The center of mass is at the middle of the length
The head is the end that leads the motion
The handle is longer, so it pulls the center its way

items.q: Where is the center of mass of the three clamps, measured from the 0 end of the stick, in meters?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the plain average of the three positions. Weight each position by its mass, then divide by the total mass.
Value: that is Σm·x, in kg·m. Divide it by the total mass, 1.20 kg, to get a position in meters.

items.q: Clamp 3 (0.70 kg) is moved from the 0.90 m mark to the 0.30 m mark. Where is the center of mass now?
options: At about 0.32 m, closer to the 0 end
At about 0.07 m, closer to the 0 end
Still at 0.67 m, since the total mass is unchanged
At about 0.50 m, the middle of the stick

items.q: The clamps are back where the table shows. Where must a fourth clamp of mass 0.60 kg be placed so that the center of mass of all four is at the 0.50 m mark? Give the position in meters from the 0 end.

mistakes.why: Value: placing the new clamp at 0.50 m does not move the center of mass to 0.50 m; it pulls it only partway there. Solve Σm·x ÷ Σm = 0.50 m for the new position.
Value: the total mass must include the new 0.60 kg clamp (1.80 kg), not only the first three.

items.q: Suppose the meterstick is not negligible: it is uniform, with a mass of 0.12 kg. Compared with 0.67 m, the center of mass of the stick and the three clamps is
options: a little closer to the 0.50 m mark
unchanged, since the stick's mass is spread evenly
a little closer to the 1 m end
exactly at the 0.50 m mark

items.q: Where is the center of mass of a thin, uniform rectangular sheet of metal?
options: Where its two lines of symmetry cross
At one corner, where the measurements start
Halfway along its longer edge
At its heaviest corner

items.q: A 2.0 kg ball sits at x = 0 and a 6.0 kg ball at x = 0.40 m, joined by a rod of negligible mass. Where is the center of mass, in meters?

mistakes.why: Value: 0.20 m is the midpoint. That is the center of mass only for equal masses; weight each position by its mass.
Value: the masses are swapped. The center of mass is closer to the heavier ball, which is at 0.40 m.

items.q: Three small objects lie on a level floor: 1.0 kg at (0, 0), 1.0 kg at (2.0 m, 0) and 2.0 kg at (1.0 m, 2.0 m). What is the y-coordinate of their center of mass, in meters?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the plain average of the three y-values. Weight each by its mass: the 2.0 kg object counts twice.

items.q: Where is the center of mass of a thin, uniform metal ring?
options: At the center of the ring, where there is no metal
Somewhere on the metal, where the mass is
At the top of the ring, above its middle
Nowhere, since the middle of the ring is empty

items.q: In which situations can you treat the system as a single point object at its center of mass, ignoring its internal structure? Select all that apply.
options: Predicting where a spinning football lands after a long throw
Explaining how a cat twists to land on its feet
Explaining why a bicycle's pedals turn its back wheel
Explaining how bending your knees lets you jump higher

items.q: A student chooses as her system a cart, a hanging block and the string that joins them. Which of these belongs to the surroundings?
options: Earth
The string
The hanging block
The cart's wheels

items.q: Ball 1 (mass m) is at x = 0 and ball 2 (mass 3m) is at x = d, on a light rod. If the mass of ball 2 is doubled to 6m, the center of mass
options: moves from 3d/4 to 6d/7, toward ball 2
moves from 3d/4 to 3d/2, twice as far out
stays at 3d/4, since the spacing is the same
moves from d/4 to d/7, toward ball 1

items.q: Put the steps for finding the center of mass of a few point objects along a line in order.
options: Choose an origin and a positive direction
Write each object's mass and position
Multiply each mass by its position and add the products
Divide that sum by the total mass

items.q: How many forces act on the loaded sled?
options: Four
Three
Five
Two

items.q: Which label correctly describes the friction arrow on the sled's free-body diagram?
options: F_f, snow on sled
F_f, sled on snow
F_f, rope on sled
F_f, Earth on sled

items.q: A student's free-body diagram of the sled shows five arrows: F_T (rope on sled), F_f (snow on sled), F_N (snow on sled), F_g (Earth on sled) and an arrow to the right labeled v. What should she change?
options: Remove the arrow labeled v
Remove the friction arrow, since the sled moves
Add an arrow for the force of motion
Remove F_N, since F_g already covers the snow

items.q: The rope pulls the sled with a force of 55 N, and the net force on the sled is 30 N to the left. The vertical forces cancel. How large is the friction on the sled, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: that subtracts the sizes as if the net force pointed right. The net force points left (−30 N), so friction must be larger than the rope's 55 N.

items.q: Which free-body diagram matches the bucket while it rises at a constant speed?
options: F_T up and F_g down, the same length
F_T up, longer than F_g down
F_T up, F_g down and a lifting force up
F_T up alone, since the bucket rises

items.q: What is the weight of the 4.0 kg bucket of sand, in newtons? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

mistakes.why: Value: 4.0 is the mass in kg. Weight is a force: multiply the mass by g.

items.q: Which object exerts the upward force on the bucket?
options: The rope
The person's hands
Earth
The sand inside it

items.q: The person stops pulling and holds the rope so the bucket hangs at rest. How does the free-body diagram change?
options: It does not change: F_T and F_g, equal in size
F_T shrinks, since the bucket is no longer rising
F_T disappears, leaving F_g by itself
F_g grows, since the bucket is now at rest

items.q: In physics, a force is best described as
options: a push or pull from an interaction between two objects
something an object carries along while it moves
the speed an object has in a given direction
the amount of matter an object holds

items.q: Which of these forces acts at a distance, without the objects touching?
options: The weight of a falling apple
The pull of a rope on a crate
The push of a floor on a box
The rub of a road on a sliding tire

items.q: A block rests on a ramp tilted 30° above the horizontal. In which direction does the normal force on the block point?
options: Perpendicular to the ramp's surface, away from it
Straight up, opposite the weight
Up the ramp, along its surface
Straight down, into the ramp

items.q: Two students push a cart along a hallway. One pushes 60 N to the right; the other pushes 25 N to the left. What is the size of the net horizontal force from the two students? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that adds the sizes. The pushes point in opposite directions, so give one a negative sign before adding.

items.q: A 5.0 kg box sits at rest on the floor while a student presses down on its top with a 20 N force. The upward and downward forces on the box are equal in size. What is the normal force from the floor on the box, in newtons? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

mistakes.why: Value: that is the weight alone. The normal force equals the weight only when nothing else pushes up or down; here the hand pushes down too.
Value: the hand pushes down, adding to the weight, so it adds to the normal force.

items.q: An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg on Earth, where g = 9.8 m/s². On the Moon, g = 1.6 m/s². Which describes her mass and weight on the Moon?
options: Mass 80 kg; weight about 130 N
Mass 80 kg; weight about 780 N
Mass about 13 kg; weight about 130 N
Mass about 13 kg; weight about 780 N

items.q: A hockey puck slides across level ice after leaving the stick. Friction and air resistance are negligible. Which arrows belong on its free-body diagram? Select all that apply.
options: F_g, Earth on puck, down
F_N, ice on puck, up
The force of the stick, forward
The force of motion, forward

items.q: A driver in a car with a dead battery sits inside and pushes hard on the dashboard. The car does not move. Which explains why?
options: The push is between two parts of the same car-and-driver object, so nothing outside pushes it
The push is too small to overcome the car's weight
The dashboard is rigid, so a push on it has no effect
The car moves forward a little and the seat pushes it back

items.q: The 6.0 kg block pushes on the 2.0 kg block with a force of 6.0 N to the right. What force does the 2.0 kg block exert on the 6.0 kg block?
options: 6.0 N to the left
6.0 N to the right
2.0 N to the left
18 N to the left

items.q: The student instead pushes the 2.0 kg block to the left with the same 24 N, so that it pushes the 6.0 kg block. How does the force between the blocks compare with before?
options: It is larger, since it now speeds up the 6.0 kg block
It is the same, because the student's push is the same
It is smaller, because the 2.0 kg block is lighter
It is zero, because now the push comes from the other side of the pair

items.q: Choose the two blocks together as the system. Which forces are internal to that system? Select all that apply.
options: The 6.0 kg block on the 2.0 kg block
The 2.0 kg block on the 6.0 kg block
The student's hand on the 6.0 kg block
Earth on the 2.0 kg block

items.q: Why can the 24 N push be used to find how the two-block system's center of mass moves, without knowing the force between the blocks?
options: The forces between the blocks are internal and cancel
The force between the blocks is too small to matter
The force between the blocks acts on the lighter block, not the heavier one
The two blocks move apart, so they do not interact

items.q: While the truck and car speed up, how does the force of the rope on the car compare with the force of the rope on the truck?
options: They are equal in size and opposite in direction
The force on the car is larger, since the car is pulled
The force on the truck is larger, since the truck leads
They are equal in size and point the same way

items.q: A student says: "The truck pulls the car forward, so the car must pull the truck backward with a smaller force, or they would not speed up." Which response is correct?
options: The pulls are equal; the road pushes the truck forward harder than the rope pulls it back
The student is right: the car pulls back less hard than the truck pulls forward
The two pulls are equal, so they cancel and the truck and car stay at one speed
The car exerts no force on the truck, since it is the car that is being towed

items.q: The truck's tires push backward on the road. What is the third-law partner of that force?
options: The road pushing forward on the tires
The rope pulling backward on the truck
Earth pulling down on the truck
The truck pushing forward on the rope

items.q: The truck and car later move at a constant speed, with the tow rope still tight. Which describes the rope's forces now?
options: It pulls the car forward and the truck backward, with one tension
It pulls the car forward but no longer pulls on the truck
It pulls the truck forward and the car backward
It pushes the car forward and pulls the truck backward

items.q: Which pair of forces is a third-law pair?
options: Earth pulls a ball down; the ball pulls Earth up
Earth pulls a book down; a table pushes the book up
A rope pulls a crate right; the floor rubs the crate left
A hand pushes a door; the hinge pushes the door back

items.q: A book rests on a table. A student says the normal force on the book and the book's weight are a third-law pair because they are equal and opposite. What is wrong with this claim?
options: Both act on the book, so they are not partners
The two forces are not equal in size
The two forces point in the same direction
Nothing: the two forces are a third-law pair

items.q: A 1000 kg car hits a 0.10 g bug. How does the force of the car on the bug compare with the force of the bug on the car?
options: They are equal in size
The car exerts the larger force
The bug exerts the larger force
The car exerts a force but the bug does not

items.q: An ideal string runs over an ideal pulley and holds a 3.0 kg block at rest in midair. The other end is tied to the floor. What is the tension in the string where it is tied to the floor, in newtons? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

mistakes.why: Value: halving assumes the pulley splits the tension. An ideal pulley only changes the string's direction; the tension is the same everywhere along it.
Value: an ideal string has one tension along its length; it is not doubled at the far end.

items.q: Two students hold the ends of a light rope and each pulls with 150 N in a tug of war. Neither moves. What is the tension in the rope?
options: 0 N

items.q: A horse pulls a cart. A student argues: "The cart pulls back on the horse as hard as the horse pulls the cart, so they cancel and the cart can never move." What is the best response?
options: The pulls act on different objects, so they do not cancel
The horse pulls a little harder than the cart pulls back
The two pulls do cancel, and the ground moves the cart instead
The cart pulls back on the horse after it starts moving

items.q: In the ideal string model, a string
options: has no mass and no stretch
has mass but no stretch
stretches but has no mass
can push as well as pull

items.q: A swimmer pushes backward on the water with her hands and moves forward. Which explains her forward motion?
options: The water pushes forward on her hands
Her arms push her body forward from inside
The water moves away, leaving empty space ahead of her
Her forward push on the water carries her along

items.q: What is the size of the upward pull that the two cords together exert on the sign, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: 5.0 is the mass in kg. The cords must balance the weight, mg.

items.q: What is the tension in each cord, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: that splits the weight evenly between the cords as if they were vertical. Each cord pulls at 30° above the horizontal, so only F_T sin 30° of each pull is upward.
Value: that uses cos 30°. The vertical component of a pull at 30° above the horizontal is F_T sin 30°.

items.q: Why do the horizontal pulls of the two cords on the sign cancel?
options: Equal tensions at equal angles pull equally hard to opposite sides
The cords pull up, and horizontal pulls do not affect a hanging sign
The weight of the sign cancels the horizontal pulls
The ceiling pushes sideways on the sign to cancel them

items.q: The cords are replaced by longer ones attached farther apart, so each makes a smaller angle (15°) with the horizontal. The sign still hangs at rest. How does the tension in each cord change?
options: It increases, since less of each pull is upward
It decreases, since the cords are longer
It stays the same, since the weight is the same
It increases, since the sign's weight increases

items.q: Which free-body diagram is correct for the sign?
options: Three arrows: two cord tensions up and outward, and F_g down
Seven arrows: two tensions, their four parts, and F_g down
Two arrows: one total tension up and F_g down
Three arrows: two tensions and a net force arrow down

items.q: Between 0.0 s and 2.0 s, what is the net force on the crate?
options: Zero
120 N forward
240 N forward
120 N backward

items.q: A student claims: "Between 0.0 s and 2.0 s the worker must push harder than the friction, or the crate would stop." Which evidence from the table best refutes this?
options: Push equals friction while v stays 0.80 m/s
The push rises to 150 N after 2.0 s
No velocity in the table is zero
The crate's mass stays 40 kg

items.q: What happens to the crate's velocity after 2.0 s, and why?
options: It increases, because the push now exceeds the friction
It stays constant, because the crate is already moving
It increases, because any push makes a crate speed up
It decreases, because the friction now exceeds the push

items.q: The worker pushes with 150 N for the rest of the trip, then lets go at 6.0 s. Immediately after letting go, what is the net force on the crate, in newtons? Give its size.

mistakes.why: Value: 30 N was the net force while the worker pushed. After letting go there is no push at all.
Value: the push stops when the hands leave the crate; a crate does not keep the force it was given.

items.q: According to Newton's first law, an object with zero net force on it
options: keeps a constant velocity
slows down and finally stops
stays at rest whatever happens
speeds up at a slow, steady rate

items.q: A car drives along a straight, level highway at a steady 25 m/s. Which is true of the forces on the car?
options: The road's forward push balances the resistance
The road's forward push exceeds the resistance
There are no horizontal forces, since the speed is steady
The engine's force on the car balances the car's weight

items.q: Which objects are in translational equilibrium? Select all that apply.
options: A book resting on a desk
A car pulling away from a stop sign
A ball at the top of its flight, momentarily at rest
A car rounding a curve at a steady 20 m/s

items.q: A passenger on a bus moving at constant velocity drops a coin. Where does it land, relative to the point directly below her hand?
options: Directly below her hand
Behind that point, toward the back of the bus
Ahead of that point, toward the front
Behind or ahead, depending on the bus's speed

items.q: A bus brakes hard, and a ball on the floor rolls toward the front. A rider says a force pushed the ball forward. What is the better explanation?
options: The ball kept its velocity while the bus slowed under it
The bus's floor pushed the ball forward during braking
The air inside the bus pushed the ball forward
The ball's inertia is a forward force acting on it

items.q: A 60 kg skydiver falls at a steady speed. What is the size of the air's upward force on her, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: a steady speed means the air's push balances the weight, not that it vanishes.

items.q: An inertial reference frame is one in which
options: zero net force means constant velocity
each object stays at rest
there is no gravity acting
the observer is speeding up steadily

items.q: Choose the cart, string and block as the system. What is the size of the acceleration of the cart, in m/s²?

mistakes.why: Value: that divides by the cart's mass only. The block's weight speeds up both the cart and the block, so divide by the total, 1.00 kg.
Value: that is free fall. The block cannot fall freely, because the string makes it drag the cart along.

items.q: What is the tension in the string while the block falls, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: 1.96 N is the block's weight. The tension is less than that, because the block speeds up downward, so the net force on it points down.

items.q: How does the tension in the string compare with the weight of the hanging block while the block falls?
options: Less than the weight, so the block speeds up downward
Equal to the weight, since the string holds the block
Greater than the weight, since it also pulls the cart
Zero, since the block is falling

items.q: The hanging block is replaced by one with twice the mass, 0.40 kg. How does the acceleration change?
options: It rises by less than a factor of 2
It doubles exactly
It stays the same as before
It increases by more than a factor of 2

items.q: Why can the tension be left out when the second law is applied to the cart-string-block system as a whole?
options: Both ends of the string pull on objects inside the system
The tension is too small to change the acceleration
The tension acts in the same direction as the weight
The pulley removes the tension from the system

items.q: Which conclusion do trials 1 to 4 best support?
options: For a fixed mass, the acceleration is proportional to the net force
For a fixed mass, the acceleration is the same at any force
For a fixed mass, the acceleration grows faster than the force
For a fixed mass, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the force

items.q: Use trials 1 to 4: a graph of acceleration against net force is a straight line through the origin. What is its slope, in kg⁻¹ (equivalently m/s² per N)? Use trials 1 and 4.

mistakes.why: Value: 2.0 kg is the mass, the reciprocal of the slope. The slope of a against F is 1/m.

items.q: Compare trials 4 and 5. What does doubling the mass do at the same net force?
options: It halves the acceleration
It doubles the acceleration
It leaves the acceleration unchanged
It reduces the acceleration to a quarter

items.q: In trial 3 the net force is 3.0 N. At the moment the reading is taken, the cart is moving to the left. What can you conclude?
options: It speeds up if the net force also points left
The net force points left, as the cart moves left
It is speeding up, as there is a net force on it
Its velocity is constant, as the force is constant

items.q: A net force of 12 N acts on a 3.0 kg box. What is the size of the box's acceleration? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that multiplies the force by the mass. The acceleration is F_net divided by m.

items.q: A 1200 kg car speeds up from rest to 15 m/s in 5.0 s along a straight, level road. What is the size of the net force on the car, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: that multiplies mass by velocity. The second law uses the acceleration, Δv/Δt = 3.0 m/s².
Value: that is the car's weight. The net force along the road comes from its acceleration.

items.q: A 2.0 kg box is pulled across a floor by a horizontal 15 N force. Friction on the box is 6.0 N. What is the box's acceleration, in m/s²?

mistakes.why: Value: that uses the 15 N pull alone. Friction pulls back, so subtract it to get the net force.
Value: friction opposes the pull, so subtract it rather than add it.
